Some went to Omarska, some went to Trnopolje, so I really couldn't see anymore if anybody stayed behind or not. I actually boarded a bus that was going to Trnopolje. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you stayed in Trnopolje for about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes. Until the 21st of August more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your wife and children manage to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes. My wife and the children did leave, but not from Prijedor but from Trnopolje in freight railway cars that would transport cattle before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did she manage to leave before you to the territory under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You reached the area of Travnik via Vlasic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived, were you militarily engaged by Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: When I came to Travnik, I was very ill. I couldn't walk. I couldn't stand on my feet, on my legs. I was exhausted, undernourished. I sought medical help which was not really readily available in Travnik. They were encircled. They couldn't provide anything like that, so I had to ask for help outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was not mobilised anywhere or -- nor did I wear a military uniform, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the military authorities help you? Did you leave Bosnia and Herzegovina or did you remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina for some time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes, they heeded my request. I asked to go for medical treatment in Croatia and that's where I was transferred, to Croatia for medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you militarily engaged in the territory of Croatia until the end of the war at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: No. I spent a short time in Croatia, perhaps two weeks or so, and then later, I went to Slovenia. My brother came to get me, and then my wife came to Slovenia to join me, and then I left farther away, together with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm going to finish by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, one of the previous answers of the witness was: "And I was not mobilised anywhere or -- nor did I wear a military uniform, as they say." That means not engaged in any army activities. Why ask that twice? There's no need to do that. Please put your last questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that question referred to the answer by the witness that he went to Croatia during the war, so I just wanted to deal with that question in line with the suggestions that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness said "anywhere." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Traldi, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time would you need? Because I'll first check with my colleagues whether we have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one or two questions for the witness. And how much time would you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I only have two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two questions only. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Taci, I have two questions for you. You repeatedly said that you had no knowledge after you had returned to your place. Now, in the proffer of testimony I read the following: "He heard some announcements on Radio Prijedor saying that the population in Kozarac should surrender, that the Serbs were a peaceful people, that they should live together, and that the power should be turned over to the Serbs." That line suggests that you were able to listen to the radio. Because, earlier, when asked about rendering any arms, you said, Well, we had no contact whatsoever, we couldn't know. Here in your proffer of evidence you say that you were listening to Prijedor Radio. Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. When I said that I listened to the radio, I said that the children that were going to school in Prijedor, they would go there. The phones were working. There was electricity when I arrived from Croatia. However, little by little everything was shutting down. Information, local transport, the schools, the electricity, the water. Everything was shut down. After that, we didn't have any more information or radio or anything like that. We didn't get any information or communication with Prijedor or from anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say it changed over time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question - and also my last question - is the following. You say you observed from room number 2 what happened outside not through a window but through the door through which you entered and left. Does that mean that the door in room 2 was ajar, that you -- it was slightly open? It was not locked?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: The door was not locked. Afterwards, they placed a kind of iron fencing there in place of a door. But there was no door there, so I could get near that opening and observe what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say there was no door. It was just an opening where a door was supposed to be. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes. There had been a door there before. Then they took down that original door. And then they welded some bars there so that we couldn't go out at night. It was locked. But we could get some air through that door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you saw the events through that -- those bars, if I -- is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And room 3 was not treated in a similar way. There still was a door, if -- did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes. Room 3 did have a door. I don't remember the colour or anything like that now. And that room was much smaller than room number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Traldi, if it's a matter of a couple of minutes, then we'll ... and then we take a break after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, at temporary transcript page 30, you told Mr. Stojanovic that "... only Muslim police remained ..." in the Kozarac police force. Could you tell the Trial Chamber at about what time did the Kozarac police become all Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact time because I didn't have any contacts with the policemen. I didn't have anything in common with them. I don't know how many of them there were. In any case, it was in my estimate that those who remained were Muslim police officers. Then also some of them arrived from Prijedor because none of the Muslim policemen could remain in Prijedor, or in Kozarac. So they all came to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "those who remained," sir, do you mean those who remained as of May 1992, as of the middle of May, as of June? Can you estimate the time for us?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you exactly, but it was when the children stopped going to school, when the Serbian forces captured Prijedor, and then they tried to get the people in Kozarac to surrender, to put up that flag, and I think that already by that time, there were no other -- there were no members from other ethnic groups in the police force anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, at pages 42 and 43 of today's temporary transcript, Mr. Stojanovic asked you about Duca, Cupo, and Kajin. At paragraph 9 of your statement, you say Kajin wore a camouflage uniform. Did you ever see Duca or Cupo wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SAFET TACI
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Cupo wearing the shirt from the uniform, but I did not see Duca in a military uniform, no. Meaning that he was wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. I see, Mr. Stojanovic, that the questions by the Bench and in re-examination have triggered no need for further questions. Mr. Taci, this concludes, then, your evidence in this case. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, and we resume at 10 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, which will be taken by whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Camille Bibles will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles, so you will take the witness. I think the witness could already be escorted close to the courtroom, I would say. Meanwhile, we'll deal with another matter; that is, the administrative hearings as suggested by the Prosecution. Mr. Lukic, last Friday you said, I think, that you are not objecting but I left it open whether you wanted to make any further submissions. Now I do not know whether you wish to do so or not, or that you say, Well, we just do not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On what, Your Honour? [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Administrative hearings on witness scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't object. The only thing we wanted to raise right now, Your Honour, is that maybe we will not be able to tell Your Honours and the Prosecution the exact amount of time we need for the cross-examination at that moment since we would learn only then who would come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that point. And I don't think that that in itself is objecting against following the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And any information, however imprecise, is better than what we're doing now, which is simply making decisions based on no information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber has no objection to discussing upcoming scheduling issues, as suggested by the Prosecution, but only so long as it does not interfere with finishing the testimony of witnesses. We would not like to have the witness stay for a weekend because we so urgently had to discuss the scheduling issues. And the Chamber expects the Prosecution therefore to proactively to raise any scheduling matters at an appropriate time, and certainly the end of a cyclus would certainly be one of those moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could make a suggestion. If before Friday Mr. Lukic were able to fill in the estimates for the first four weeks when we return, the hearing could actually be quite brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, you're invited to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly, there is an issue to raise with the Trial Chamber prior to the witness's actual arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to address the attention that this Trial Chamber has brought to this next witness's testimony, and I believe it was placed on the record on the 9th of July of this year. Your Honour, we do intend to rely very heavily on adjudicated facts 460, 462 to 465, 468 to 476 with respect to Manjaca in leading this witness's testimony. We will also rely heavily on adjudicated facts 1141 through 1144 and 1146 with respect to it the takeover the Sanski Most. As well, to some degree, the adjudicated facts in 1165 to 1169, and certainly with respect to 1190 and 1192. However, as the Trial Chamber has alluded, as part of our prosecutorial judgement, we do make an evaluation of each witness and their evidence. Now, in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the case of this particular witness, after reviewing the evidence and in consultation with Mr. Groome, we have determined that there is some evidence that he has that we would lead in full. So unless there's a -- there are additional concerns from the Trial Chamber, then we can go ahead and bring in Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I make this observation, and I've done that several times, if you say these are the adjudicated facts, we'd like to know, but nevertheless it remains the responsibility of the Prosecution to clearly define for itself what the matters are for which no evidence needs to be led, because the Chamber doesn't take responsibility for that. The Chamber, at the very end, will just look at what was proven and, as far as adjudicated facts is concerned, apart from challenges, whether -- if you rely on the adjudicated fact it could not beyond what the adjudicated facts tell us. If that is clear, then if there's no other matter, the witness could be escorted into the courtroom. Or is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, that's it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Begic, I take it. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text will now be handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begic. Pleas be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, you will first be examined by Ms. Bibles. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution. You find her to your right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Begic. Could you introduce yourself with your full name and your age, please.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Rajif Begic. I was born on 23rd September 1967. So I'm 45.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you also have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They call me Raho.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us which village and municipality in which you were born?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born and grew up in the village of Plevci, Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe us the hamlet or the villages that are in the area of Sanski Most where you lived?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around Sanski Most, to the right of the river Sana, there was Kljevci village, which is a large village with several hamlets in it; such as Begici, Kenjari, Cosici, Stojnovci, and just after Kljevci came Hrustovo village, Vrhpolje, Tomina river, Caplivo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Your Honours, if we could bring 65 ter 08755 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review a map with the villages and their ethnic composition in 1992 from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry Madam Bibles, what's the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Looking at the map that is on the screen in front of you, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Does it fairly and accurately depict the villages of Sanski Most as they existed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And directing your attention to the lower right-hand portion of the map, do you see the area in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Villages Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Begici, Kenjari. That's the area where I lived, in the lower right corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 08755.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 08755 becomes Exhibit P162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P162 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us in the time period before the conflict in Bosnia what the relationships were like between Muslims and Serbs in your area?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the village of Kljevci and with other villages around Kljevci, interpersonal relations were very good. We grew up in villages with a mixed population. We went to school together. We socialised among ethnic communities, and before the war there had been no incidents on a nationalist grounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of your godparents?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: They are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us who they are?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vid Krlic and Andza Krlic. Our neighbours from Begici village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you have a close relationship with them up through 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: You could say so. We were close. We shared some agricultural machinery. We owned them jointly. We were friends. They were my godparents, my godmother -- my godmother cut my hair when I was born, and according to our customs, thus, she same my godmother.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I am going to be limiting my questions in this regard in reliance on adjudicated facts 1141 to 1144.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In May of 1992, did you surrender any weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: My neighbours from Begici village handed over some weapons. I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you able to hear the radio broadcasts directing Muslims to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several days before the 25th of May, the local radio broadcast that local villages, including Kljevci, should hand over any weapons they had at the closest Serb check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During any time in 1992, were you involved in any actions to defend your village or any other territory?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No. There were no such actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We're aware that your village was first attack in May of 1992. Can you tell us what date that was?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: It was the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know which military unit controlled the area in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: It was a part of the 6th Krajina Brigade that was based in the primary school, the four-year school, in Kljevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that unit was in -- in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of that unit was Mile Mijatovic, and he once visited us at the hamlet. He introduced himself, so we knew who commanded that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what date he came to your village?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date, but it was a couple of days before the 25th. Perhaps the 23rd or the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us how he introduced himself to you and your family?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. One day, accompanied by a soldier, both of them armed, we -- they came to our house with the intention of meeting all the residents of that village. He said where he hailed from, whose son he was, and we knew that, although he wasn't living in Kljevci by that time. We knew his father. And that conversation over coffee was not long. He told us a couple of things about the situation, and then he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did he say what army he was a commander in?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said he had a unit from the 6th Krajina Brigade that was based at the school, which we had not known, and he said he was in charge of that part of Kljevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did he say if he was with the JNA or the VRS or what military organisation?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: He did not tell us exactly the name of his unit. He just said it was the 6th Krajina Brigade. I did not hear him mention the VRS or the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know who the komandant for the 6th Krajina Brigade was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade was Branko Basara.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And how is it that you know that?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, after doing my military service, I was, myself, part of the reserve force of the 6th Krajina Brigade. We all knew that, as far as the reserve force is concerned, our area was covered by the 6th Krajina Brigade. Just before the events, a month or two before, Branko Basara attended a meeting in Tomina, where he met locals from the surrounding villages, where he introduced himself. He was wearing a uniform. And the issue came up of where to put up some units and where to deploy some tanks and howitzers in the area, so that's when I met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I don't believe that I've asked you this yet, but what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At the end of May 1992, did you come to know a soldier whose last name was Palija?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met a soldier by the name of Jadranko Palija.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What was your understanding as to where he came from?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I did not know that soldier, Jadranko Palija before. Once, driving my tractor by a Serb check-point, I was stopped by my Serb neighbours, and Jadranko Palija was among them. They talked to me briefly while he searched the tractor checking whether I had any weapons in there, and I heard someone address him as Jadranko. At that time I did not know his last name, Palija.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And did you later come to understand where he had come from?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was already on the next day when my godmother Andza, passing by, stopped at our house for coffee and he said that a soldier was visiting her house by the name of Jadranko Palija and that perhaps he had a thing for her daughter. So that's the first time I heard his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is that how you learned where he came from?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. When she was talking about him, she stressed that he lived in Croatia, and as the war was moving to Bosnia, he fled to Bosnia and he was assigned to be in that locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And by that locality, was that your area?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean that locality. More precisely, that first check-point that was put up next to Begici village. He was assigned to man that check-point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment for the clarity of the record. You told us about the check-point where you were stopped with your tractor and somebody addressed this man we were -- you were talking about as Jadranko without mentioning his family name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And then, in that case, on page 62, line 17, the second word should be deleted or redacted. Only Jadranko was mentioned. You learned his last name only later. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the completeness of the record, I notice that on the one screen the numbering of the lines is slightly different from the other one, but I think it is clear it is the words before it says "at that time I did not know his last name, Palija." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The -- can you describe for us what the soldier, Palija's attitude towards the Muslims in the area was?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not see that soldier again after those days. That was my first meeting with him, and then the next time I saw him it was already 31st of May, so I don't know if he had had any contacts in the meantime with my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During the time-period from the 25th of May to the 31st of May, can you describe what life was like for you and your family?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. After this first incursion of soldiers into our hamlet, until the 31st, we lived in fear. On the 25th, when they entered the hamlet, they mistreated and beat people. And in the days that followed, fear reigned, and we were completely at a loss what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Where were you when your village was attacked on the 25th of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: On the 25th, when the troops were coming into our hamlet, I was outside my house with my brother. When they came by, it was in fact a young man who was running ahead of them, saying, The army is coming. My junior -- my younger brother, Munib Begic, and I ran to the river to hide there, not far from the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you able to see or hear what was going on with your village?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: We were not able to see, but we could hear everything. Perhaps not every word, but we could clearly hear what was going on around our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe just briefly what it was that you were able to hear from the river?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could hear our old aunt trying to defend her old husband, Huso, who was 75. And next to them we could hear small children crying. We could hear soldiers shouting, Get into the garage. We're going to kill you now. There were many voices at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: How long did the attack last?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Not long. Not longer than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm now directing your attention to the 31st of May of 1992. I'd like you to think about the soldiers that entered your village on that date. Were there soldiers that you did not know?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 31st of May, I recognised some of the soldiers whom I had known from before, from the town and school, but most of them were not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us whether you knew the soldier who ordered the separation of women and children from the men?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know that soldier. All I could see was that he was in command of that unit that was in Begici on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was there any fighting or resistance from the Muslims in the community?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened to the men in your community as the separations occurred?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the locals from Dizdarevici and Donji Begici were brought to us, I lived in Gornji Begici, the men who were found in the basement of Ekrem Begic were lined up outside the house. As we were coming to Gornji Begici, it was ordered already that women and children should go to one side, whereas the men should form a column to join the men who had already been lined up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And did the men do as they were told?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did as we were told. We had to line up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And can you describe how the column was organised, the column of men?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: After separating the women and children, and even one underaged boy managed to join the group of women and children with his mother, they lined us up in a column two by two and told us to go towards Vinogradi.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: How many armed soldiers escorted your group of men away?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Our column that was going towards Vrhpolje was escorted by many armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know who the leader of that group of soldiers was?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: The one who was in charge of escorting the column was Jadranko Palija.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At that time did you know any of the other soldiers that he was commanding?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised some of the young men who were from Sanski Most, from the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us if you knew where you were going?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. While we were still standing in Begici, the officer who was in charge of those soldiers on that day said the soldiers would escort us to the bridge over the Sana river where buses were waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Approximately how far did you -- would you go from Begici to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: At least 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the ages in your group, the ages of the Muslim men? Just roughly. The youngest and the oldest.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The youngest in the group was called Enes Dizdarevic, and at the time he was between 15 and 16 years old. Edin Begic, my youngest brother, had been put aside with his mother because he seemed younger but he was the same age. The oldest one was Sacir Begic who was over 70 years old, and there was Miralem Celic [as interpreted], who was perhaps a year or two younger.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As your group walked towards the bridge, did you go by some other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not far from the Begici hamlet that we were moving away from, we came across a group of soldiers who were resting by the road that we were travelling down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And how did they react to your group?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Jadranko stopped our group there, and then these soldiers, about 30 of them, insulted us, cursed us. Someone even said that we should be killed there on the spot. But they did not beat us on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that location?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Not long. A few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And which direction did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: After that, Jadranko Palija ordered the column to move on in the same direction, towards Vinogradine about 100 metres away from that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you able to move at the pace that you wanted to -- to move, or you and the group?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were ordered to maintain a steady pace, although we had to bring these old people along with us too. Because at one point in time, Jadranko Palija said that if someone shooted at the column from the surrounding villages, they would all kill us. And that is why it was necessary for us to move rapidly. Some were not able to keep up and we therefore had to help them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. Who had the most trouble keeping up?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Sacir Begic and Miralem Ceric found it most difficult. Miralem, after about 100 metres, had pain and felt pain in the heart and his son tried to take care of him. We had to carry Sacir Begic. Irfan and myself grabbed him by the arms and helped him, while the other people in the column were able to move ahead on their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: While you were moving towards the bridge in this column, could you describe for us what was happening in the area?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we approached the Hrustovac [as interpreted] station where there were a number of houses, we noticed that all the houses were on fire. You could see a weapon firing. You could see soldiers sitting by the road. Some were cursing. Others drinking. Some were stealing cars or items from cars. It was ugly. An ugly scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: How many smaller bridges did you cross before getting to Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, as we were approaching Hrustovac station there was a small bridge over the Glibaja river, that we then had to cross a bridge over the Sanica river. That was in Hrustovo station. And then we headed onto this other bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In that area that you've just described --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Near Vrhpolje, interpreter's correction. A bridge near Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: After crossing that area, could you describe for us how Miralem Ceric was doing?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that point in time, when we arrived at Hrustovac station we could see that Miralem Ceric was out of breath, and he was breathing with difficulty and it would have been good for him to have a break. He was breathing with difficulty and moving with difficulty, although his son Enes was helping him to -- to walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what, if anything, Palija did as a result of his difficulties?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time when we were crossing the -- a bridge over the Sanica river, right by the bridge on the left-hand side there was a slaughter-house, an abandoned slaughter-house. At that point in time, as we were passing by that slaughter-house, Jadranko took Miralem Ceric and his son Enes aside. In fact, he took them into that old slaughter-house. When the three of them entered the slaughter-house, I saw Jadranko Palija taking out his pistol and following them inside, in fact. I then heard a shot, and I saw Jadranko Palija coming out of the slaughter-house and putting the pistol back into its holster. He then joined the column which hadn't stopped advancing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you ever see either of these two men again?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did Palija take anyone else from the column after that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to that question. May I ask you to clarify. Sorry. You said you heard a shot. One shot or more shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, at that point in time, all the houses in the vicinity of the bridge were on fire and the bricks were actually cracking. I heard a shot which was a pistol shot. I'm sure that I heard one shot. I didn't hear any other shots. Perhaps because of the noise being produced by the houses that were on fire and by the bricks that were cracking. But I am certain that I heard one shot being fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did Palija take anyone else from your column after that?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The column continued towards the Vrhpolje bridge and then we had to get to the main road that was about 250 metres from that location. And at the exit that leads to the main road, Jadranko took Ismet Kurbegovic out of the column. He took him to the other side of the road and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did he -- did Palija say anything to Ismet before he killed him?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Jadranko took him aside. He pointed his gun at him, and he said, For the last time, I'm asking you, where is your sniper? Ismet said he did not have a sniper rifle of any kind, and this man then shot him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you actually see the shot?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Bibles. The shot or the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will rephrase that to the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you see the shooting?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: He killed him with one shot from the gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was this the same pistol that you saw him holster a few minutes before?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did Palija come back to your group at that point?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This all happened quite quickly. The column hadn't really moved very far, and you could see him walking -- walking by with the column.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And what happened to Ismet's body?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: His body remained lying by the road, by a stop sign. His body remained lying there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When you came within 10 metres of the Vrhpolje bridge, could you see who was on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. From a certain distance you could see that there were a lot of soldiers on the bridge. It wasn't really possible to see them clearly until we had actually reached the bridge. Having reached the bridge, I could recognise some of those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were there buses on the bridge when you could first see it?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you got very close to the bridge, did any vehicles come alongside your group?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time, just before we reached the bridge, a military van, a small military van, arrived from the direction of Kljuc. There was one driver in it. Though the van was advancing at the same speed as the column, and then the driver in the van told Jadranko Palija to get in and sit down to his right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened after he got in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: After Jadranko Palija got into the van, the column continued advancing on the left-hand side, and at that point in time Irfan Begic and myself were still helping Sacir Begic to walk. Elmedin Begic instinctively grabbed Sacir Begic to help him move, and then Jadranko Palija who was sitting in the van called out to Irfan Begic and told him to move in front of the van and to go to the other side, the side on which he was sitting. When Irfan Begic crossed over to the other side of the road in front of the van, I had a look to the right, to my side, and I saw that Jadranko Palija didn't say anything, but when Irfan arrived by the window, he shot him from his pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At that point, what were you thinking?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were terrified by what we had seen. Appalled by it. We had to go to the bridge. We had to continue to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could exhibit 65 ter 06367 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph depicts the Vrhpolje bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is this the same bridge that was there on the 31st of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is it -- and could you tell us the name of the river that we see running under the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the river Sana.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At -- I'm going to ask you to make some markings on this photograph but not just yet, and I would ask for the colour red to be used with the pen. Do you know which direction this river flows?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. From left to right. If you look at the photograph, it's from left to right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take the pen and draw a small -- I'm sorry, just a moment. I'm going to ask that you draw a small arrow on the river indicating which direction of river flows, please.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher otherwise assist the witness in using the eraser as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the river flow from the left on the picture to the right. Is that -- is it possible to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, before we continue, 65 ter 06367 is described on our list as photo of the Vrhpolje bridge annotated by the witness, but are there any previous annotations or is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there do not appear to be any annotations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So we will need to correct that description of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Once it is admitted, if you tender it, then, of course, there are annotations. So perhaps you have anticipated on what might happen in court. But I was just wondering whether I missed something. But let's proceed. I've heard your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you see the road that you entered the bridge from?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you please take the pen and mark a number 1 on the road that will show us the direction that you came from?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, it's -- apart from you do not come from a direction but you come from a place and then move in a certain direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do I understand that, looking at this picture, you came to the bridge from the left on the road, as we see it, moving to the right and thus arriving at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'll have you go ahead and just put the pen down for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As your column came onto the bridge, could you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we approached the bridge, we were going down the left side of the road. And when we reached the bridge, we were ordered to go to the right part of the fence on the bridge and to line up in a column, one by one, in the middle of the bridge at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would this have been on the up-river side of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the right side of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you -- after you lined up, what did they have you do next?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: After we had lined up, we were ordered to take our shoes off and our clothes. Not all of our clothes, but most of them. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. And could you describe for us, as you did that, what the soldiers were doing?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we started approaching the bridge, they started cursing and maltreating us. And then when all the people had taken their clothes off, one or two soldiers searched the people who were lined up there. They asked us whether we had any money on us or any weapons, and they asked us to display what we had, if we had anything, and then they started beating certain people, certain individuals, on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When you finished -- which clothing did you take off?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I took off my trousers, my shoes, some remained in their trousers. Some didn't take their shoes off. Well, in fact, everyone took their shoes off. But, on the whole, there were a lot of clothes piled up on the bridge. Some would remain wearing two T-shirts, two shirts. They didn't order us to take everything off.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And what were you still wearing?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: I had a short white T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As the beatings were happening, did someone start to talk about going off the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what happened after the beatings started?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were beating Hakija Begic, Mile Begic at the time. They were also beating Fuad Begic. And then at one point in time they started beating everyone. So, on the whole, everyone was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you as to what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. While this beating and cursing and -- was going on, while they were insulting us, Kaurin, Nenad, Nenad Kaurin, said aloud that they had to kill 70 Muslims on that day because seven Serbian soldiers had been killed during that period in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What were you thinking at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC
utterances.text: We were frightened. We had been beaten up. It was cold. We were no longer thinking about buses arriving there. We were just waiting to see what the fate of the group would be. We'd been abandoned to our fate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, having just glanced at the time, I'm wondering if this would be a point at which we should take a break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you think this is a suitable moment. I take it, then, that the next line of questions would take more than the two or three minutes we have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, do you intend to have more markings? Because there's a bit of a problem if we adjourn for the day, that we can't keep it as it is, the photograph of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would tender exhibit 65 ter 06367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is now a photograph of Vrhpolje bridge marked by the witnesses, isn't it. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06367 as marked by the witness in court becomes Exhibit P163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And P163 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Begic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. But before you leave, I'd like to instruct you that should not speak with anyone or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is your testimony as you have given it today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 4th of September, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be resumed on Tuesday, the 4th day of September, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.15 p.m.,
